title: Index Law Puts Contracts and Human Counsel Behind Mike-1
summary: Index Law Puts Contracts and Human Counsel Behind Mike-1
body_markdown:
[Index Law](https://indexlaw.com/) is launching Mike-1 as a way for companies to assign legal work, not just ask legal questions. The AI agent is intended to understand a business's documents, prepare and revise contracts, and involve experienced human lawyers when a matter requires them.


The name needs a qualification that the company itself makes explicit: Mike-1 is not a licensed or practicing lawyer. It assists with research, drafting, review and workflows. Qualified people remain necessary where professional legal advice or representation is required. Index Law is the company; Mike-1 is its product.


The Fall 2026 Y Combinator startup is beginning with contracts and corporate work for startups and growing businesses. Founder Quddus Pativada frames the problem from the client's side: finding counsel, repeatedly explaining the company and coordinating the work can remain difficult even when lawyers gain better software.


Mike-1's proposed workflow starts with a concrete matter. The agent reviews an agreement against the company's priorities, explains issues and prepares redlines. It can then help with negotiation and document revision, keeping the work moving toward a version ready for signature while allowing the customer to review and approve along the way.


[Watch the original launch video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nmJhvLenZKk) .


Human escalation is part of that workflow rather than a separate directory of lawyers. Index Law says Mike can bring in a vetted specialist with the relevant documents and context already prepared. Customers can use the agent directly, work alongside their existing counsel or obtain support from a lawyer supplied through the company.


The other proposed advantage is continuity. Contracts, past negotiations and company information stay together so a later matter does not begin with a blank conversation. For a business handling repeated commercial agreements, the important context can include decisions already made about risk and terms, not just the wording of the latest document.


Index Law reports that it has worked with startups and larger companies, turned around contracts in less than an hour and quoted some work at up to 80% below traditional alternatives. Those are company-reported examples, not a general service guarantee. The announcement does not provide enough detail about the agreements, comparison quotes or review requirements to apply the figures to every legal matter.


That distinction also separates fast document production from legal judgment. Generating a redline is not the same as deciding whether a business should accept the resulting allocation of risk. Index Law identifies knowing when to involve a person as one of the harder problems behind the product.


Pativada's launch describes personal and entrepreneurial experiences with expensive legal work as the motivation for building Mike-1. The resulting commercial ambition is to make the engagement feel more like assigning a task to software while preserving access to specialist counsel when needed.


The immediate question is how consistently that combination works across real contracts and corporate matters. A useful agent has to keep the company's context straight, make the status of its work clear and escalate appropriately. Index Law is proposing a different front door to legal services, but the quality of the outcome still depends on the judgment and review behind it.
